description: Earth locations that simulate the environmental conditions of permanent Moon bases and Mars settlements, you're looking for places known as Planetary Analog Sites.
summary: Project Mission Earth is a responsive field guide comparing Earth locations with Moon and Mars exploration questions. It combines NASA’s Planetary Analog Explorer and lunar south-pole illumination data to examine Kīlauea and California lava caves for lunar geology and field operations, and the Atacama Desert and McMurdo Dry Valleys for Mars instrument and surface studies. Visitors can filter analog profiles by destination and see similarities alongside limits. Every profile links to NASA sources so readers can trace the evidence. The project shows how Earth fieldwork can reduce some exploration risks, while explaining why no Earth site reproduces low gravity, vacuum, space radiation, or another world’s atmosphere. It is a literature-based prototype, the website and qualitative comparisons were built.
details:
PROJECT DESCRIPTION — PROJECT MISSION EARTH

What it does and how it works

Project Mission Earth is a responsive, source-linked field guide to Earth locations that help researchers investigate selected Moon and Mars questions. Visitors can filter the analog profiles by destination. Each profile states the location, the specific research use described by NASA, and the environmental mismatch that limits the analogy. The guide uses the lunar south-pole region and Jezero Crater as reference environments. Jezero is identified as a NASA robotic exploration site, not a selected human settlement location.

The comparison is qualitative and evidence-led. It does not calculate a best site, assign numerical similarity scores, run a GIS overlay, or recommend where to establish a base. The Moon examples focus on volcanic fieldwork and lava-cave detection research; the Mars examples focus on dry-soil instruments and cold-desert surface processes.

Benefits and intended impact

The site makes several NASA analog examples easier to compare and gives students and general audiences a direct route from each claim to its source. It explains why terrestrial fieldwork can help researchers practice procedures, examine landscapes, and test instruments in relevant settings. Its intended impact is educational: help people understand how analog research can reduce selected exploration risks while making clear that field analogs cannot replace laboratory, engineering, or space-based tests.

Tools, software, and hardware actually used

The website is built with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript as a static site. The editable PowerPoint deck was authored with Node.js and the Artifact Tool presentation library. NASA pages, NASA mission imagery, and the NASA Goddard Planetary Geodesy, Geophysics and Geochemistry Laboratory’s Lunar Polar Illumination resource were used to curate the comparison. The LRO LOLA resource is cited for context; this prototype does not analyze its raster files.

Creativity and design choices

Instead of presenting one “best Earth twin,” the project matches each location to a specific question and places the mismatch beside the similarity. The Moon and Mars filters let a reader move between destinations without implying that a single score can combine geology, terrain, operations, resources, and environment. NASA imagery and linked references make the evidence traceable.

Environmental, accessibility, and cost considerations

The artifact is digital and static, so it requires no field campaign, travel, sampling, or new physical materials. Bundled images avoid autoplay video and reduce dependence on third-party image services. The page uses semantic HTML, descriptive image text, keyboard-operable filter buttons, visible focus states, responsive layouts, strong text contrast, and a reduced-motion preference. Hosting energy was not measured.

Energy, temperature, altitude, atmosphere, and cost are discussed as factors that matter for future analog campaigns and off-world operations, not as measured outputs of this project. NASA reports that some permanently shadowed regions near the lunar south pole can reach about −203°C, while nearby sunlit areas can be much warmer; these conditions vary by location. Mars has a thin atmosphere made mostly of carbon dioxide, and the Moon has an extremely tenuous exosphere. The Moon’s gravity is about one-sixth of Earth’s; Mars gravity is also lower. Earth analogs therefore cannot reproduce vacuum or near-vacuum, low gravity, space radiation, or the full thermal and atmospheric conditions. Altitude and site access vary by location and have not been normalized or ranked here.
